core: Imagery as sensory language across channels: visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, kinesthetic/kinetic
Imagery versus figurative language: a literal sensory detail is still imagery
How imagery creates vividness, emphasis, and experience (showing versus telling)
Analyzing an image field or pattern across a passage rather than one isolated word
Brief genre notes: imagery in poetry, fiction, drama, and nonfiction
supporting: Taxonomy of imagery types, including kinesthetic/kinetic and organic imagery
Selectivity and particularity in effective imagery; avoiding clichés
Imagery as one element among others in textual analysis
outOfScope: Mood (atmosphere; sibling topic, referenced but not taught)

claims.claim: Imagery is language that appeals to the senses to create mental images and sensory experience, including sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
Imagery invokes the five senses — visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile — to create mental images; individual images can be classified by the sense they engage.
Imagery need not be figurative; a literal sensory detail such as “the kettle whistled” is imagery. Figurative language often enhances imagery but is not required for it.
Imagery creates vividness by showing rather than telling: sensory details engage readers through their senses and bring an experience to life.

Writers repeat words, ideas, and images to call attention to them and signal that they matter, so analysis should track an image field—the pattern of related sensory details across a passage—rather than a single isolated word.
Effective imagery is selective and particular: specific details engage readers more than stock phrases, and clichés are easy for readers to ignore.

Imagery works across genres, reaching readers through different channels: in poetry it is often load-bearing; in fiction it builds scenes and can recur across chapters; in drama it must arrive through dialogue and stage directions; in nonfiction writers select sensory details to make factual experience vivid.

positions: Poetry Foundation's glossary defines imagery as elements invoking the five senses, “using vivid or figurative language,” a broad phrasing that can blur imagery with figurative language.
OpenStax and CLC writing texts treat imagery as sensory language that figurative devices often enhance but do not require.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches imagery as sensory language and presents figurative language as an optional enhancement, while noting that definitions vary in breadth.

positions: Some definitions restrict imagery to the five classic senses.
Other references add kinesthetic (movement) and organic (internal sensation) imagery.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the five senses as the core and kinesthetic/kinetic as a widely listed extension, without claiming a universal taxonomy.

unsupportedExistingClaims: “Imagery is a foundational concept in English & Literature” (generated boilerplate with no subject content)

“College courses use imagery as a building block for later discussions” (unsupported generality)

correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic boilerplate with a sourced sensory-language definition of imagery.
Corrected the implicit equation of imagery with figurative language by teaching that literal sensory details are imagery.
Added the full sensory taxonomy, including kinesthetic/kinetic imagery.
Added the image-field/pattern method for analysis, replacing the draft's vague “apply to a simple scenario” objective.
Tightened out-of-scope boundaries: symbolism, metaphor/simile, mood, and tone are referenced only as sibling topics.
rightsIssues: None. All sources were used reference-only; no source prose, student examples, or literary passages are reproduced. The CLC chapter includes student-authored examples reproduced there with permission; this lesson does not copy them.
